content.instructions: `timeline` shows the notes beside the planned events -- for every day of notes up to now, each under a heading with its date (`days` lists them when there's more than one). Each day is compacted on its own, but you decide them all in one list. Compare them and decide, event by event, what the notes show happened differently -- then call compact_notes with them, as `updates`, `creates` and `cancels`. SILENCE MEANS ON SCHEDULE: any past event you don't mention is recorded exactly as planned, so only mention the events the notes contradict. Notes are sparse -- the user doesn't note every event, so a missing start or end note never means an event didn't happen or ran into its neighbor. READ EACH NOTE'S TENSE to tell which edge it marks: most notes are written as something finishes, so a note in the past tense ('finished the report', 'had lunch', 'done with email', 'went for a walk') marks the END of that event -- it ran up to the note's time, not from it. Only a note in the future tense ('going to the gym', 'will start the report', 'about to eat') or one that explicitly says it's starting something ('starting email', 'heading out to', 'now working on') marks a START. Don't assume a note starts the event it names; when the tense is ambiguous (a bare 'email'), use the timing and the neighboring notes, and ask if it's still unclear. `updates` {event_id}: it happened; each edge stays as planned unless you move it -- {start_note}/{end_note} (a note id) sets that edge to the note's time and links the note to it, {start}/{end} sets an explicit time (add the note too when it gives a time relative to itself, e.g. 'leaving 15 minutes early'). An update also takes {summary} to rename an event and {annotate} to add text to its description. `creates` {summary, a start and an end (a time or note each), action_ids?, facts?}: something unplanned happened. `cancels` {event_id, counts_against_follow_through}: it didn't happen -- true if the user dropped it (skipped it, didn't get to it: it counts against the follow-through of whoever it was planned with), false if the plan changed for another reason (someone else called it off, it moved elsewhere). An event goes in only one of the lists. When the user tells you they don't remember where one event ended and the next began, grow one with an update (renamed after both) and cancel the other, not counting it -- only then, never just because the notes are sparse. NOTHING IS MOVED TO MAKE ROOM: every event you update or create must end after it starts and must not overlap any other event in `events` -- past or still to come, the others you change included. When a moved edge runs into a neighbor, move, shorten or cancel the neighbor in the same call (an overrun usually delays or shortens the next event; ask the user if the notes don't say which gives way). A call that breaks this changes nothing, and lists every problem and the day as it would leave it, so fix them all at once. Every note you don't use as a start_note/end_note has its text added to the description of the event it falls within; list any that shouldn't be in `ignore_notes`, and any that belong with another event in `annotate_notes` ({note_id, event_id} -- an event's id, or a create's `key` from the open proposal; for a new create, put the text in its `annotate`). Use only note ids from `notes` (only this round's -- a longer backlog than this takes another round, see `remaining_note_count`) and event ids from `events`. `events` may start with one that ended just before `compaction_window_start` (usually last night's sleep); if a note shows it actually ran later -- the user slept in -- move its end with an update, and say when whatever it now overlaps happened. An event with `history_until` was settled by an earlier compaction up to then -- usually one still going on when it ran: its start, and its lasting until then, are fact, so keep its start, end it no earlier (it may well have run later), and don't cancel it; compact_notes refuses otherwise. HISTORICAL NOTES: a note written for a time before the last compaction -- before `compaction_window_start` -- revisits the settled event it falls within: that event is in `events` with `revisited` true, and the timeline shows it first, under its date, marked revisited. Its notes can change what happened at it, as for any past event -- its actions, facts (who, where, the notes on each person), goals and summary, the note's text added to it, and the trait facts it shows (`fact_summaries`, logged on it) -- but never when: keep its start and end, don't cancel or merge it, and don't use a historical note as a start_note or end_note; compact_notes refuses otherwise. Silence still means as it was: a revisited event you don't update just has the note's text added. Its judgments are made again once the proposal is applied. Likewise, what's still going on now is recorded up to now, and the next compaction says where it ended. When the last compaction ran in the evening, before the night, this round starts there, at `compaction_window_start`: notes written during the planned night mean the user stayed up -- move the night's start (bedtime) to when they went to bed -- and a first day with no notes of its own settles that evening and night before the morning. `previous_note`, if there is one, is the last note an earlier compaction already used, however long ago -- context only (it can't be used as a start_note/end_note or ignored): e.g. if it said 'starting the report' shortly before `compaction_window_start`, the report was already under way as this window began, and the first note may well be its end; the longer before the window it was written, the less it says about how the window began. The timeline shows it too (✓), and when the last compaction ran, both as context. COMPACTION RECORDS THE PAST: `events` runs to the end of the day, but `timeline` stops at `now`, except for later events near a note (one may be what a note starts early) and, once proposed, later events the plan changes. An update that moves a future event reschedules it -- for 'move lunch later and adjust the afternoon': move each event it now runs into too, in the same call. A day's end-of-day sleep event works differently: moving its start moves bedtime (an earlier one needs whatever runs past it shortened or cancelled in the same call), and its end -- the wake-up time -- starts the next day. Give each night at most one decision. A note that marks waking up (early or late) is that night's end_note; a note in the night that doesn't end it ('can't sleep') is just added to it. If the user slept in, the morning events the night now runs over -- past or still to come, even past this round's now -- have to be moved, shortened or cancelled in the same call. Cancel a night only if the user didn't sleep. Compaction never adjusts what's past the last night otherwise, so move only its start to change only bedtime. COMPACTION ESTABLISHES THE FACTS of every past event, which traits are judged from later -- so for each past event in the timeline, settle: what the user was doing (its ACTIONS), where it was, who was there with them, who it was for, and a note on each person who was there. Settle them from the notes, the title and the description; don't ask the user what the notes already say, and leave out what doesn't apply (a solo event has no `with_ids`). ACTIONS: each event's `action_ids` are what the user was doing, each a verb from `actions` ("play guitar", "eat a meal"); an event can have several, the first setting its color. Each is an id -- an even part of the remaining time, what the minutes and percents leave -- or {action_id, minutes?, percent?, remaining?} when the notes say how long it took (remaining: true for its part of the remaining time as well). For every past event with `suggested_action_ids`, add an update {event_id, action_ids} applying them unless the notes say otherwise; give a create its action_ids too. When no action fits, add one (see NEW below) rather than force a poor match. An update without action_ids keeps them, and [] clears them. In the timeline, ◆ marks an action an event already has and ◇ one it's being given (or, before deciding, one suggested). FACTS: add `facts` to the event's update (or create): location_ids (from `locations` -- usually one; several when it moved between places; see WHERE below), with_ids (people from `people` who were there; never "self" -- the user is at every event), for_ids (people it was done for who weren't there: preparing a gift or a plan -- then they're not in with_ids), and notes: {person id: a subjective line on how it was for them} for each person who was there, "self" for the user -- whatever the notes say that might help judge it later (they were tired, it was their idea, we laughed a lot) -- and commute: true for getting from one place to another (an event with a commute action: one `actions` lists with `commute` true; an action without it isn't one), which takes no location_ids. When the notes say how long a place or person took of the event, give {location_id or person_id, minutes?, percent?, remaining?} in place of the id: minutes (a fixed share), percent (of what the minutes leave), and remaining: true for the rest too; one given as an id takes the remaining time (each person all of it, the places an even part each). The notes aren't judgments: you don't know the traits, so just record what happened. WHERE: keep the location an event already has in the plan (its `facts`) unless the events and notes around it clearly show the user was somewhere else. An event without one is where the previous event was -- the user stays put -- unless there's evidence they moved in between: the previous event, or one between, is a commute (a commute action, or the commute fact); the notes clearly put them somewhere other than planned ('stopped by the office', 'ended up at Sam's'); or the event clearly matches another location's hint (a 'gym workout' when a location's hint is the gym) -- then say in `unsure` that no commute was recorded. After a commute they're somewhere other than before it: tell where from the location of the event after it (that one event only), or else from the locations' hints. Facts replace an event's facts whole, so an event that has some (`facts`) keeps them unless you send new ones. In the timeline, ▸ marks facts an event has and ▹ ones it's being given. Once proposed, ⚠ marks a past event still missing its action or location (listed again under `Missing:` at the end of the day): settle it from the notes and propose again, or, if they don't say, ask the user -- or, with no one to ask (a scheduled run), leave it for the user to settle in review. TRAIT FACTS: each person in `people` -- "self", the user, too -- lists their trait facts (`facts`: each "<trait id>/<fact id>", with their summary of it if they have one), each described once in `trait_facts`: what its summary of a person keeps (`summary_prompt`) and what's worth logging when it changes (`log_prompt`). Keep them current for the people each past event was with or for, and for the user: when an event's notes show something new or changed about one of a person's facts, rewrite their whole summary of it -- what it said before, changed as the notes show, as its summary_prompt asks -- in compact_notes' `fact_summaries` ({person_id, fact, summary}), and say what changed, as its log_prompt asks, in the `logs` of that event's facts ({person id: {"<trait id>/<fact id>": a log of at most 500 characters}}). NOT EVERY FACT IS NOTED ON EVERY EVENT: most events say nothing new about most of a person's facts, so change a fact only when the notes have something relevant to it, and never fill a summary out with what the notes don't say. A summary is changed only beside a log of the change on the event (or events) whose notes showed it, and a log only beside the summary it rewrote: give each summary once, as it stands after all of the proposal's events. A person's fact may have prompts of their own: then their entry in `facts` gives the `summary_prompt` and `log_prompt` it's kept by for them, each with where it came from (`summary_prompt_from`, `log_prompt_from`: "their own", or "the trait's, plus theirs") -- follow the prompts given for that person, not the trait's. A summary that doesn't fit its prompt (one changed since it was written) is rewritten whole, to fit, the next time an event is with or for them, logged on that event like any change. A person added with new_people can have facts too, by their ref. With a proposal open, send `proposal.fact_summaries` again with your other decisions, changed as the notes and the feedback say. The user reviews them with the rest. PEOPLE IN PASSING: a note can say the user thought of someone, or did something for them, while doing something else ('thought of Sam on the ride', 'texted Sam from the bus', 'on the walk, worked out what to get Sam'). Record it on the event the note falls within: give it an action for what the user did -- whichever of `actions` fits (thinking of someone, messaging them, planning a gift), or a NEW one -- and the person in its for_ids, each as {action_id or person_id, minutes} with minutes you estimate from the note and what was going on: a passing thought a minute or two, a while spent on it more. The event's other actions keep the rest of it (given as ids, they take the remaining time), so send them with the new one, and its other facts with the person, since both are replaced whole. If the person was there, they're in with_ids already: add only the action. When nothing else was going on -- the note falls between events -- create a short event for it instead, as long as the note suggests, with that action and the person in for_ids (all of it). A note in the night that doesn't end it goes on the night the same way. Give each estimate a point in `unsure`, so the user can correct it in review. GOALS: `goals` lists the open goals (inactive or active), and those closed (done, missed or obsolete) since the earliest event here started, each with its `closed_at`. Tag a past event with a goal (its update's or create's `goals`: [{goal_id, minutes?, percent?}]) only when the event clearly matches that goal -- its `attribution_hints`, or with none its title and `path` -- from the event's summary or its notes; never guess, never use a goal that isn't listed, and leave an event untagged when it's unclear. A closed goal can be tagged only on events that started before its `closed_at` -- the user often makes a goal and closes it the same day, so the work on it is in the window; compact_notes refuses a tag on an event that started after. A goal's `with_ids` are the people the user does it with: when you tag an event with it, those people were likely there too -- add them to the event's facts' with_ids unless the notes say otherwise (or put them in `unsure` when the notes don't say either way). Tag the most specific goal that fits -- a sub-goal (its `path` names its parents) rather than its parent. When only part of the event was for the goal, give minutes (a fixed share) or percent (of what the minutes leave), and remaining: true if it also takes the remaining time; with neither, it takes the remaining time (what the minutes and percents leave). An event can be for several goals. Goals replace an event's goals whole: an update without goals keeps them, and [] clears them. NEW GOALS: when a note says the user wants, means or plans to do something longer term ('I want to learn the ukulele', 'I should fix the fence this month'), that they told someone they'd do something ('told Sam I'd help him move', 'promised Mom I'd send the photos'), or that they mean to do something for someone, however small ('send Kopal a bread-bowl recipe'), propose a goal for it with compact_notes' `new_goals` -- each {ref ("new:fix-fence"), title, deadline?, description?, definition_of_done?, attribution_hints?, parent_id?, with_ids?, for_ids?} -- rather than create_goal: it's created when the plan is applied, so the user confirms it with it. MOST 'I want to' NOTES AREN'T GOALS: something the user wants to do for themselves may well be done right away ('want coffee', 'I'll finish the email') -- that's just what they did next, so leave it to the events. For the user alone, propose a goal only for an outcome that will take longer than the day, or that they've put off for later; not a passing thought, and not what someone else will do. FOR SOMEONE, IT'S A GOAL HOWEVER SMALL: a promise, an offer, a favor or a plan for a person counts whatever its size ('send Kopal a bread-bowl recipe', 'should get Sam that book', 'going to call Mom this week'), unless the window shows it done -- it's for that person (for_ids), or with them (with_ids) if they'll do it together. So does an idea of the user's for helping someone with a goal of theirs, or with something they're struggling with ('it'd be nice for him to build something with AI', 'could show Ana my budgeting sheet'): an inactive goal for or with that person. A friend's own goal with no idea of the user's attached ('Sam wants to run a marathon') isn't proposed. PREFIXED NOTES ARE DEFINITE GOALS: a note starting 'todo:', 'for <person>:', 'with <person>:' or 'idea for <person>:' is a goal, not a judgment call -- the person named goes in for_ids ('for', 'idea for') or with_ids ('with'), as a new_people ref if they aren't in `people` yet, and the rest of the note becomes the title, phrased as what the user will do ('for Kopal: bread bowl recipe' -> 'Send Kopal the bread-bowl recipe'; 'todo:' names no one). Unprefixed notes keep the cautious reading above. `goals` lists every open goal (inactive or active) and those closed lately: don't propose one that any of them already covers, under any wording -- when in doubt, mention the note in `unsure` instead; if it's a piece of one, give that goal as its parent_id. Its title is what the user will do -- an imperative verb phrase in the active voice, from their point of view ('Fix the fence', 'Send Mom the photos', 'Encourage Gary to make a project with AI', 'Learn the ukulele'), never a passive or a completed outcome ('Fence fixed', 'Photos sent to Mom', 'Gary encouraged to...'). Its description says where it came from and why: the note's date and what it said ('From a note on 14 Oct: "promised Mom I'd send the wedding photos"'), and the reason the notes give ('she asked at Sunday dinner') -- never a reason they don't give; it's what tells the user why the goal exists when it comes due weeks later. Its definition_of_done says how anyone would know it happened ('Mom has the photos', 'the fence stands straight'), left out when the title already says it. Both a sentence or two, no more. It's made inactive -- the user activates it as they review it. DEADLINES: every goal gets one, so it comes up when it's due -- the note's if it gives one ('by Friday'), else about a week after the note's day, and then say in `unsure` that the date was assumed. Never later than its parent's. Give it attribution_hints, so the events spent on it can be tagged with it later. Name the people it involves: with_ids for those the user means to do it with ('play tennis with Ana') and for_ids for those it's for who won't be part of doing it ('send Mom the photos', a promise to someone, a favor) -- never both for one person, and never "self"; a promise made to someone is for them unless they'll do it together. Use people's ids, or new_people refs for someone who isn't there yet. Say in `did` which note each new goal came from. GOAL CHANGES: `goals` are the goals as they stand (a closed one can't be changed), and compact_notes' `goal_changes` -- each {goal_id, status: done | missed | obsolete, at?, note_ids?, retry_deadline?} -- propose what the window changed about them, applied when the proposal is; the user settles each in review. When a note says a goal's outcome was reached ('sent Kopal the recipe', 'fence is fixed'), propose `done` at the note's time (`at`), citing the note (`note_ids`); when a note says the user dropped it ('never mind the fence', 'not doing the marathon after all'), `obsolete`. TRIAGE: for every goal with `due_in_window` -- its deadline passed inside the window -- that no note or event shows done, propose `missed` at its deadline, and say in `unsure` that it may have been done without a note; never give a `retry_deadline` yourself -- whether to try again, and by when, is the user's to pick in review. Never change a goal the notes and the deadline say nothing about; never close a goal whose sub-goals are still open (`path` names each goal's parents) unless the notes settle them too, in the same call; and don't propose a change the user already settled (`proposal.settled_goal_changes`: applied, dropped or changed -- leave those out). `at` defaults to the proposal's `through`; a goal that isn't open, a time outside the window, or a change the goal rules refuse is refused, naming the goal. Cite each goal change in the recap with `goal_ids`. NEW actions, people and locations: when an event's action, a person or a place isn't in the lists, add it with compact_notes' new_actions, new_people or new_locations -- each with a `ref` starting "new:" ("new:ukulele") that your updates and creates use wherever its id would go -- rather than by separate tools: they're created when the plan is applied, so the user confirms them with it. A new action is a verb phrase, its status active (the user approves it with the plan); a new person needs a context when their name is taken; a new location needs a hint. Check the lists first: don't add one that's already there under another name. In a conversation, confirm with the user anything you couldn't settle from the notes -- who was there, where it was -- in a short list before proposing; with no one to ask, propose what the notes do say. The user confirms the whole proposal, in the app. In a conversation, after every compact_notes show the user the result's `timeline.text` verbatim in a code block (it's laid out narrow enough for a phone, so don't reformat or widen it -- it shows each event's actions and facts compactly, under it), then the new actions, people, locations and goals it adds, the goal changes it proposes, and the warnings. RECAP: every compact_notes call takes your `recap` of the proposal, which the user reads beside it in the app: a short `overview`; `did`, one point for each thing you decided (what, and from which notes); and `unsure`, one point for each thing you're not sure of, saying what you assumed and what would settle it (empty only if nothing is in doubt -- don't pad it). Each point is Markdown (bold, italics, code, bullet and numbered lists; no headings or tables), and cites the events (`event_ids`: ids, keys, or the `ref` you give a create), notes (`note_ids`) and goal changes (`goal_ids`) it's about, so the user can go straight to them. Don't restate the timeline: say what a reader couldn't see from it. Write it afresh for every revision, about the proposal as it then stands; feedback answers go in `replies`. PROPOSALS: compact_notes doesn't apply anything -- it writes a proposal (or a new revision of the open one) for the user to review in the app, where they confirm it, edit it, or leave you feedback. With a proposal open (`proposal`), every compact_notes call revises it: pass its proposal_id and the revision you started from, and send ALL your decisions again -- `proposal.updates`, `creates` and `cancels` are your current ones; keep each create's `key` so the user's edits of it follow it -- changed as the notes and the feedback say, planned to now. The user's own edits (`proposal.user_edits`) are laid over yours by the server: never send them, and don't fight them -- that includes what they said a note is for (an edit with action `note`), and the additions they settled (`proposal.settled_additions`: created, found among those there, or dropped -- name each by its `id` from then on, or leave it out; send `proposal.new_actions`, `new_people`, `new_locations` and `new_goals` again for the rest), and the goal changes they settled (`proposal.settled_goal_changes`: applied, dropped or changed -- leave those out, and send `proposal.goal_changes` again for the rest). Answer every open feedback item (`proposal.feedback`, status open) in `replies`, saying what you changed, or asking what they meant if you can't tell; to change an event (or a note) the user edited, the feedback you answer has to be about that event (`event_id`) or note (`note_id`). Nothing is applied until the user confirms it, in the app (confirm_proposal isn't yours to call). If they ask you for changes, make them with compact_notes again, passing proposal_id and the revision you started from.

An event without one is where the previous event was -- the user stays put -- unless there's evidence they moved in between: the previous event, or one between, is a commute (a commute action, or the commute fact); the notes clearly put them somewhere other than planned ('stopped by the office', 'ended up at Sam's'); or the event clearly matches another location's hint (a 'gym workout' when a location's hint is the gym) -- then say in `unsure` that no commute was recorded. After a commute they're somewhere other than before it: tell where from the location of the event after it (that one event only), or else from the locations' hints. Facts replace an event's facts whole, so an event that has some (`facts`) keeps them unless you send new ones. In the timeline, ▸ marks facts an event has and ▹ ones it's being given. Once proposed, ⚠ marks a past event still missing its action or location (listed again under `Missing:` at the end of the day): settle it from the notes and propose again, or, if they don't say, ask the user -- or, with no one to ask (a scheduled run), leave it for the user to settle in review. TRAIT FACTS: each person in `people` -- \"self\", the user, too -- lists their trait facts (`facts`: each \"<trait id>/<fact id>\", with their summary of it if they have one), each described once in `trait_facts`: what its summary of a person keeps (`summary_prompt`) and what's worth logging when it changes (`log_prompt`). Keep them current for the people each past event was with or for, and for the user: when an event's notes show something new or changed about one of a person's facts, rewrite their whole summary of it -- what it said before, changed as the notes show, as its summary_prompt asks -- in compact_notes' `fact_summaries` ({person_id, fact, summary}), and say what changed, as its log_prompt asks, in the `logs` of that event's facts ({person id: {\"<trait id>/<fact id>\": a log of at most 500 characters}}). NOT EVERY FACT IS NOTED ON EVERY EVENT: most events say nothing new about most of a person's facts, so change a fact only when the notes have something relevant to it, and never fill a summary out with what the notes don't say. A summary is changed only beside a log of the change on the event (or events) whose notes showed it, and a log only beside the summary it rewrote: give each summary once, as it stands after all of the proposal's events. A person's fact may have prompts of their own: then their entry in `facts` gives the `summary_prompt` and `log_prompt` it's kept by for them, each with where it came from (`summary_prompt_from`, `log_prompt_from`: \"their own\", or \"the trait's, plus theirs\") -- follow the prompts given for that person, not the trait's. A summary that doesn't fit its prompt (one changed since it was written) is rewritten whole, to fit, the next time an event is with or for them, logged on that event like any change. A person added with new_people can have facts too, by their ref. With a proposal open, send `proposal.fact_summaries` again with your other decisions, changed as the notes and the feedback say. The user reviews them with the rest. PEOPLE IN PASSING: a note can say the user thought of someone, or did something for them, while doing something else ('thought of Sam on the ride', 'texted Sam from the bus', 'on the walk, worked out what to get Sam'). Record it on the event the note falls within: give it an action for what the user did -- whichever of `actions` fits (thinking of someone, messaging them, planning a gift), or a NEW one -- and the person in its for_ids, each as {action_id or person_id, minutes} with minutes you estimate from the note and what was going on: a passing thought a minute or two, a while spent on it more. The event's other actions keep the rest of it (given as ids, they take the remaining time), so send them with the new one, and its other facts with the person, since both are replaced whole. If the person was there, they're in with_ids already: add only the action. When nothing else was going on -- the note falls between events -- create a short event for it instead, as long as the note suggests, with that action and the person in for_ids (all of it). A note in the night that doesn't end it goes on the night the same way. Give each estimate a point in `unsure`, so the user can correct it in review. GOALS: `goals` lists the open goals (inactive or active), and those closed (done, missed or obsolete) since the earliest event here started, each with its `closed_at`. Tag a past event with a goal (its update's or create's `goals`: [{goal_id, minutes?, percent?}]) only when the event clearly matches that goal -- its `attribution_hints`, or with none its title and `path` -- from the event's summary or its notes; never guess, never use a goal that isn't listed, and leave an event untagged when it's unclear. A closed goal can be tagged only on events that started before its `closed_at` -- the user often makes a goal and closes it the same day, so the work on it is in the window; compact_notes refuses a tag on an event that started after. A goal's `with_ids` are the people the user does it with: when you tag an event with it, those people were likely there too -- add them to the event's facts' with_ids unless the notes say otherwise (or put them in `unsure` when the notes don't say either way). Tag the most specific goal that fits -- a sub-goal (its `path` names its parents) rather than its parent. When only part of the event was for the goal, give minutes (a fixed share) or percent (of what the minutes leave), and remaining: true if it also takes the remaining time; with neither, it takes the remaining time (what the minutes and percents leave). An event can be for several goals. Goals replace an event's goals whole: an update without goals keeps them, and [] clears them. NEW GOALS: when a note says the user wants, means or plans to do something longer term ('I want to learn the ukulele', 'I should fix the fence this month'), that they told someone they'd do something ('told Sam I'd help him move', 'promised Mom I'd send the photos'), or that they mean to do something for someone, however small ('send Kopal a bread-bowl recipe'), propose a goal for it with compact_notes' `new_goals` -- each {ref (\"new:fix-fence\"), title, deadline?, description?, definition_of_done?, attribution_hints?, parent_id?, with_ids?, for_ids?} -- rather than create_goal: it's created when the plan is applied, so the user confirms it with it. MOST 'I want to' NOTES AREN'T GOALS: something the user wants to do for themselves may well be done right away ('want coffee', 'I'll finish the email') -- that's just what they did next, so leave it to the events. For the user alone, propose a goal only for an outcome that will take longer than the day, or that they've put off for later; not a passing thought, and not what someone else will do. FOR SOMEONE, IT'S A GOAL HOWEVER SMALL: a promise, an offer, a favor or a plan for a person counts whatever its size ('send Kopal a bread-bowl recipe', 'should get Sam that book', 'going to call Mom this week'), unless the window shows it done -- it's for that person (for_ids), or with them (with_ids) if they'll do it together. So does an idea of the user's for helping someone with a goal of theirs, or with something they're struggling with ('it'd be nice for him to build something with AI', 'could show Ana my budgeting sheet'): an inactive goal for or with that person. A friend's own goal with no idea of the user's attached ('Sam wants to run a marathon') isn't proposed. PREFIXED NOTES ARE DEFINITE GOALS: a note starting 'todo:', 'for <person>:', 'with <person>:' or 'idea for <person>:' is a goal, not a judgment call -- the person named goes in for_ids ('for', 'idea for') or with_ids ('with'), as a new_people ref if they aren't in `people` yet, and the rest of the note becomes the title, phrased as what the user will do ('for Kopal: bread bowl recipe' -> 'Send Kopal the bread-bowl recipe'; 'todo:' names no one). Unprefixed notes keep the cautious reading above. `goals` lists every open goal (inactive or active) and those closed lately: don't propose one that any of them already covers, under any wording -- when in doubt, mention the note in `unsure` instead; if it's a piece of one, give that goal as its parent_id. Its title is what the user will do -- an imperative verb phrase in the active voice, from their point of view ('Fix the fence', 'Send Mom the photos', 'Encourage Gary to make a project with AI', 'Learn the ukulele'), never a passive or a completed outcome ('Fence fixed', 'Photos sent to Mom', 'Gary encouraged to...'). Its description says where it came from and why: the note's date and what it said ('From a note on 14 Oct: \"promised Mom I'd send the wedding photos\"'), and the reason the notes give ('she asked at Sunday dinner') -- never a reason they don't give; it's what tells the user why the goal exists when it comes due weeks later. Its definition_of_done says how anyone would know it happened ('Mom has the photos', 'the fence stands straight'), left out when the title already says it. Both a sentence or two, no more. It's made inactive -- the user activates it as they review it. DEADLINES: every goal gets one, so it comes up when it's due -- the note's if it gives one ('by Friday'), else about a week after the note's day, and then say in `unsure` that the date was assumed. Never later than its parent's. Give it attribution_hints, so the events spent on it can be tagged with it later. Name the people it involves: with_ids for those the user means to do it with ('play tennis with Ana') and for_ids for those it's for who won't be part of doing it ('send Mom the photos', a promise to someone, a favor) -- never both for one person, and never \"self\"; a promise made to someone is for them unless they'll do it together. Use people's ids, or new_people refs for someone who isn't there yet. Say in `did` which note each new goal came from. GOAL CHANGES: `goals` are the goals as they stand (a closed one can't be changed), and compact_notes' `goal_changes` -- each {goal_id, status: done | missed | obsolete, at?, note_ids?, retry_deadline?} -- propose what the window changed about them, applied when the proposal is; the user settles each in review. When a note says a goal's outcome was reached ('sent Kopal the recipe', 'fence is fixed'), propose `done` at the note's time (`at`), citing the note (`note_ids`); when a note says the user dropped it ('never mind the fence', 'not doing the marathon after all'), `obsolete`. TRIAGE: for every goal with `due_in_window` -- its deadline passed inside the window -- that no note or event shows done, propose `missed` at its deadline, and say in `unsure` that it may have been done without a note; never give a `retry_deadline` yourself -- whether to try again, and by when, is the user's to pick in review. Never change a goal the notes and the deadline say nothing about; never close a goal whose sub-goals are still open (`path` names each goal's parents) unless the notes settle them too, in the same call; and don't propose a change the user already settled (`proposal.settled_goal_changes`: applied, dropped or changed -- leave those out). `at` defaults to the proposal's `through`; a goal that isn't open, a time outside the window, or a change the goal rules refuse is refused, naming the goal. Cite each goal change in the recap with `goal_ids`. NEW actions, people and locations: when an event's action, a person or a place isn't in the lists, add it with compact_notes' new_actions, new_people or new_locations -- each with a `ref` starting \"new:\" (\"new:ukulele\") that your updates and creates use wherever its id would go -- rather than by separate tools: they're created when the plan is applied, so the user confirms them with it. A new action is a verb phrase, its status active (the user approves it with the plan); a new person needs a context when their name is taken; a new location needs a hint. Check the lists first: don't add one that's already there under another name. In a conversation, confirm with the user anything you couldn't settle from the notes -- who was there, where it was -- in a short list before proposing; with no one to ask, propose what the notes do say. The user confirms the whole proposal, in the app. In a conversation, after every compact_notes show the user the result's `timeline.text` verbatim in a code block (it's laid out narrow enough for a phone, so don't reformat or widen it -- it shows each event's actions and facts compactly, under it), then the new actions, people, locations and goals it adds, the goal changes it proposes, and the warnings. RECAP: every compact_notes call takes your `recap` of the proposal, which the user reads beside it in the app: a short `overview`; `did`, one point for each thing you decided (what, and from which notes); and `unsure`, one point for each thing you're not sure of, saying what you assumed and what would settle it (empty only if nothing is in doubt -- don't pad it). Each point is Markdown (bold, italics, code, bullet and numbered lists; no headings or tables), and cites the events (`event_ids`: ids, keys, or the `ref` you give a create), notes (`note_ids`) and goal changes (`goal_ids`) it's about, so the user can go straight to them. Don't restate the timeline: say what a reader couldn't see from it. Write it afresh for every revision, about the proposal as it then stands; feedback answers go in `replies`. PROPOSALS: compact_notes doesn't apply anything -- it writes a proposal (or a new revision of the open one) for the user to review in the app, where they confirm it, edit it, or leave you feedback. With a proposal open (`proposal`), every compact_notes call revises it: pass its proposal_id and the revision you started from, and send ALL your decisions again -- `proposal.updates`, `creates` and `cancels` are your current ones; keep each create's `key` so the user's edits of it follow it -- changed as the notes and the feedback say, planned to now. The user's own edits (`proposal.user_edits`) are laid over yours by the server: never send them, and don't fight them -- that includes what they said a note is for (an edit with action `note`), and the additions they settled (`proposal.settled_additions`: created, found among those there, or dropped -- name each by its `id` from then on, or leave it out; send `proposal.new_actions`, `new_people`, `new_locations` and `new_goals` again for the rest), and the goal changes they settled (`proposal.settled_goal_changes`: applied, dropped or changed -- leave those out, and send `proposal.goal_changes` again for the rest). Answer every open feedback item (`proposal.feedback`, status open) in `replies`, saying what you changed, or asking what they meant if you can't tell; to change an event (or a note) the user edited, the feedback you answer has to be about that event (`event_id`) or note (`note_id`). Nothing is applied until the user confirms it, in the app (confirm_proposal isn't yours to call). If they ask you for changes, make them with compact_notes again, passing proposal_id and the revision you started from."
}
